transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?

Hi, yes, thank you. Well, it's actually kind of embarrassing, to be honest, especially at my age. I feel like I should have a handle on this sort of thing by now. But what brings me in is this... this issue I'm having where I just cannot seem to stay in my chair. I keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put, and it's happening in situations where it really matters and it's starting to cause problems. 

Like, I'm a private investigator, right? So I have these long, sensitive client interviews where someone is pouring their heart out about a cheating spouse or missing corporate assets, and they really need me to be grounded. But I just... I can't stay seated. I'll suddenly stand up and start pacing or go look out the blinds, and they look at me like I don't care about their case at all. And it's not just work! I do some tutoring on the side, and I'll just pop up out of my seat in the middle of explaining a concept. Even at my Wednesday night book club—which is supposed to be relaxing, we're doing historical fiction right now, it's usually very laid back—I'm constantly up getting water, looking at the host's bookshelves, standing behind the sofa instead of sitting on it. 

People are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen to them. My friend Brenda actually made a comment about it last week at the meeting, asking if I had somewhere better to be because I kept hovering. It's just so frustrating because I *am* listening to them, I really am, I just literally cannot keep my body in the chair when I'm supposed to.
Aside from trouble sitting still, do you also find it difficult to maintain your focus on tasks or activities?

No, actually, not at all. My focus is... well, it's really quite sharp, to be honest. I mean, given my line of work, it has to be, right? When I'm on a case, I can sit there—well, I mean, mentally sit there, even if my body is doing laps around the room—and comb through bank statements, phone records, or surveillance logs for hours. I don't lose the thread of what I'm doing. It's actually one of the reasons I'm good at my job, because I can lock onto a discrepancy in a timeline and just drill down into it until I figure out what's really going on. 

And it's the same with the tutoring, you know? I'm helping these kids with algebra, and I'm completely dialed into their thought process, catching exactly where they missed a step in the equation, even if I happen to be standing by the whiteboard or pacing behind their chair while I'm doing it. I don't get distracted or forget what we're working on. And at book club, I'm the one who remembers all the character arcs and the minor plot points from three chapters ago, even though Brenda thinks I'm not paying attention just because I'm looking at a knick-knack on the mantle. 

So, no, the focus part isn't the problem. My brain is totally engaged and on track. It's just... it's just the physical part. It's like my brain is doing exactly what it's supposed to do, but my body just refuses to get the memo that we are supposed to be sitting down while we do it. I just don't have that mental drift that people talk about, you know? My mind is right there, it's just my legs that want to be somewhere else.

Do I feel... what exactly? I'm sorry, you trailed off there for a second. But if you're asking if I feel like an actual physical sensation, like a crawling or an ache or a tingle in my legs that makes me have to move them, no, not at all. It's not like that. 

I know what you mean, though, because my Aunt Susan—my mom's younger sister, she used to live in Florida but she moved back up here after her second husband passed away—she has that restless leg thing. She was always complaining about how her legs felt like there were bugs under the skin at night, and she had to get up and walk around just to make it stop hurting or feeling weird. She used to walk laps around her living room at 2:00 AM, drove my uncle crazy. 

But for me, it's nothing like that. There's no pain, no weird creepy-crawly feeling, no numbness, no tingling, nothing uncomfortable in the muscles or the nerves or anything like that. My legs feel completely normal, physically speaking. They don't hurt, they don't itch. It's just... it's just this overwhelming urge to just *be up*. It's not a reaction to a bad feeling in my legs, it's just that my body wants to be in motion. Like, I'll be sitting there, and suddenly the idea of staying in the chair just feels impossible, not because my legs are bothering me, but because I just have this energy that needs to get out. So, no, no weird physical sensations driving it, just... just me needing to stand up.
Did you experience similar issues with restlessness or having a hard time staying seated when you were a child, before the age of 12?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's funny you ask about being a kid, because... well, it's definitely not a new thing, that's for sure. 

I mean, if you were to go back and look at my old grade-school report cards—which my mother actually kept, by the way, she has this giant plastic storage tote in her basement filled with basically every piece of paper I ever touched—but if you looked at them, there is a very obvious theme. Every single year, whether it was Mrs. Gable in second grade or Mr. Harrison in fifth, the comments in the margins were always exactly the same. They would always write that I was a very bright student, which was nice of them, but then there was always this big "however" attached to it. They'd say I was bright, *but* I just couldn't stay in my seat. Or I was bright, *but* I had a terrible time waiting my turn to speak or do an activity. 

My mom actually still brings it up at family dinners. She thinks it's completely hilarious now, especially given what I do for a living as a private investigator. She always jokes that I treated every single classroom like it was an active crime scene that I just *had* to pace through to gather clues. Like I was investigating the chalkboard or doing surveillance on the pencil sharpener. 

And honestly, she's not wrong! I distinctly remember in fourth grade, we had these assigned reading times where we were supposed to sit quietly on these little individual carpet squares, and I would just end up wandering around the perimeter of the rug while I read. I wasn't trying to be bad or disruptive, I really wasn't. I just couldn't stay anchored to the little square. The teachers would get so exasperated with me, constantly telling me to sit down, sit down, sit down. So, yes, long before I was 12, this was... this was just how I operated. It's just wild to me that I'm 49 years old and I'm basically still doing the exact same thing I was doing when I was eight, you know?
